primary_topics: Remarks at the retirement celebration of Justice Santiago Javier Ranada (Court of Appeals), November 6, 2006 -- CJP speaks as a fellow retiree-in-waiting (his own retirement is 'just weeks away')

Justice Ranada's five character portraits: obedient son (fulfilled his late father's deathbed wish to become a judge); faithful husband (39-year marriage, only one love for 42 years); loving father (five children, three married, seven grandchildren); gentleman boss (soft-spoken, patient, discreet); illustrious Laoagueño

CJP's parallel with Justice Ranada: both have fathers named Artemio; both had their careers determined by their fathers; CJP refrains from using 'Jr.' so every good thing he does is credited to his late father

The salutary life: 'a salutary life, a decent job, the rare opportunity to serve the judiciary and to be remembered patriotically beyond this life' as the summary of what retiring jurists can thank for
sub_topics: Parallel introductions: 'I am also a junior because my father's name is also Artemio. But I have refrained from using Jr. after my name so that every good thing that I do may be credited to my late father, who had practically commanded me, contrary to my wishes to become a chemical engineer, to pursue a career in law.'

Justice Ranada's deathbed-wish origin story: his father, Santiago Ranada Sr., was 'a sagacious judge in Pasay City' who whispered at his deathbed that he wanted his junior to become a judge; 'having already established a successful law practice, he found the request difficult to accede to. But eventually he took the road his father had fated him to take. And so, he became a judge of the Court of First Instance in 1978.'

Faithful husband: 'Evelyn, his wife of 39 years, relates with fondness that for the past 42 years, he has had only two barbers, and most important, he has had only his one and only love for the past four decades.'
Five children, seven grandchildren: 'All of his five children finished their studies. Three of them are now married and have gifted him and Evelyn with seven grandchildren.'

Gentleman boss: 'He is soft-spoken, patient, and very discreet. He does not take offense easily, neither does he give any. During the nearly three decades he has served the judiciary, our honoree found the greatest enjoyment holding trials in his court.'

Retirement feelings: 'Justice Jun looks forward to retirement with mixed feelings of hope and fear -- 80 percent of hope and 20 percent of fear. Now that my own retirement is just weeks away, I can understand his jitters.'

The salutary life: 'like me, and all retiring jurists, Jun has a lot to thank for and look back to the years he has spent in the judiciary. On top of that to-thank-for list would be a salutary life, a decent job, the rare opportunity to serve the judiciary and to be remembered patriotically beyond this life.'

stances.claim: The 'salutary life' -- 'a decent job, the rare opportunity to serve the judiciary and to be remembered patriotically beyond this life' -- is CJP's summary of what all retiring jurists should count as their greatest gift. This is not a modest formulation but a genuinely elevated one: being remembered patriotically beyond one's mortal life is the highest form of legacy.

stances.confidence: asserted as the governing reflective evaluation

stances.claim: CJP's refusal to use 'Jr.' after his name -- so that every good thing he does is credited to his late father -- is the most original and most selfless form of filial piety in the corpus. It inverts the normal use of 'Jr.' (claiming heritage) into an act of tribute (giving credit).

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 6, 2006 at the retirement celebration of Court of Appeals Justice Santiago 'Jun' Javier Ranada -- CJP three weeks before his own mandatory retirement -- this address by CJP opens with a personal parallel: 'I am also a junior because my father's name is also Artemio. But I have refrained from using Jr. after my name so that every good thing that I do may be credited to my late father, who had practically commanded me, contrary to my wishes to become a chemical engineer, to pursue a career in law.' Justice Ranada's career similarly began with a deathbed wish: his father, Santiago Ranada Sr. (a Pasay City judge), whispered at his deathbed that he wanted his junior to become a judge; despite an established law practice, Ranada eventually honored the wish, becoming a CFI judge in 1978 and climbing to the Court of Appeals. CJP presents five character portraits: obedient son (honored the deathbed wish); faithful husband ('Evelyn relates that for the past 42 years, he has had only two barbers, and most important, he has had only his one and only love for the past four decades'); loving father (five children, three married, seven grandchildren); gentleman boss (soft-spoken, patient, discreet; 'found the greatest enjoyment holding trials in his court'); and illustrious Laoagueño. CJP notes: 'Justice Jun looks forward to retirement with mixed feelings of hope and fear -- 80 percent hope and 20 percent fear. Now that my own retirement is just weeks away, I can understand his jitters.' He closes: 'On top of that to-thank-for list would be a salutary life, a decent job, the rare opportunity to serve the judiciary and to be remembered patriotically beyond this life. Mabuhay ka, Justice Jun!'
